final_note: You walked through the three types of bonding and the structures they form.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Metal + non-metal = ionic bond.

The metal loses electrons (becomes +); the non-metal gains them (becomes -).

Na -> Na+ + e-; Cl + e- -> Cl-. The ions form a giant lattice.

Two non-metals share a pair of electrons.

Hydrogen (H2) shares one pair; oxygen (O2) shares two pairs (double bond).

Covalent bonds are strong, but forces between small molecules are weak.

Metals form a giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

This explains why metals conduct electricity and heat.

Layers slide, so metals are malleable.

options: covalent
ionic
metallic
hydrogen

mcqs.q: Which bonding involves shared pairs of electrons?
options: ionic
metallic
covalent
none

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine?
options: Sodium loses one electron to chlorine; the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attract electrostatically.
Sodium and chlorine share an electron between them.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Metals contain naturally moving protons that act as charge carriers.
Metal atoms themselves move to carry the current.
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice of positive ions, carrying charge.
